Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-25
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Laura Patel (Ionix CTO), Ethan Miles (Ionix Head of ML Infra), Priya Singh (Ionix SRE)
Links shared: perf-spreadsheet: https://drive.local/ionix/perf.xlsx ; deck: https://drive.local/ionix/rdw-deck.pdf ; SOC2 doc noted.

Summary (auto):
Quick deep dive on observed p95/p99 tail for Ionix production LLM endpoints. Focus areas: KV cache behavior, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact, streaming vs non-streaming latency, and network hop effects inside VPC. Agreed next steps: customer provides traces and topology; Redwood runs bench with KV enabled; Redwood sends SOC2 and pricing.

Topics:
- p95/p99 tail latency sources
- KV cache warm/cold behavior and prefix caching
- Batching strategies (dynamic vs fixed) and continous batching impact
- Quantization tradeoffs: int8 vs fp16 latency + accuracy
- Streaming vs non-streaming: token-at-a-time vs chunked responses
- Network hops, VPC egress, and on-prem considerations

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna focus on the tail latency stuff you saw in the dashboard, p95/p99, and dig into runtime and infra. Diego is here to run through kernel-level and runtime stuff.
[00:22] Laura Patel: Thanks Maya. yeah our users see a lot of spikes, p99's sometimes over a second on smaller 3B models and for the 13B it's... it spikes a lot. we're trying to understand whether it's batch sizing, the KV cache, or network.
[00:37] Diego Ramos: cool; brief agenda — we'll run through metrics you shared, then hypothesis: cold KV cache, batching variance, quantization path differences, and network hops. then recommended configs and a test plan.
[00:50] Ethan Miles: just FYI our infra is a VPC with transit gateway to on-prem—so there are a couple network hops for evaluation. we also do TLS termination at the ALB.
[01:05] Priya Singh: and I should call out we have autoscaling for pods so pod cold start is a variable too.
[01:12] Diego Ramos: absolutely, pod spin-up and model load are major p99 contributors if not pinned. but your symptoms sounded like sustained tail even when pods warm?
[01:22] Laura Patel: yeah it's not just a toe-in start, it's during normal load—every once in a while a request takes 800ms-1.2s while median is 80-120ms.
[01:35] Diego Ramos: okay that points at KV cache misses or routing variances. do you have prefix caching enabled today?
[01:42] Ethan Miles: we have a basic cache in front of the model but we're not using Redwood-style KV cache. it's mostly request-level caching at the app layer.
[01:51] Maya Chen: quick note — when we say KV cache in our runtime, it's the KV-cache of the model's decoder keys/values that prevents recomputing. it's different from HTTP cache.
[02:03] Priya Singh: got it, there was some confusion on our side there, thanks.
[02:10] Diego Ramos: ok, first, high level: p99 tail often breaks down to three buckets: 1) compute variance (like different kernel paths or quantized code paths), 2) caching and KV cold misses, 3) networking and scheduling delays.
[02:25] Maya Chen: and we should cover streaming — are you using streaming responses?
[02:30] Ethan Miles: yes for chat we stream token-by-token to the client, but we also have non-streamed batch endpoints for longer completion jobs.
[02:38] Diego Ramos: streaming can add latency variability depending on how the SDK and client ack boundary are implemented; also micro-batching in the runtime can delay first-token latency.
[02:50] Laura Patel: our biggest issue is the first token; sometimes it's instant, sometimes it's delayed — so first-token p95/p99 is alarming.
[03:02] Diego Ramos: that aligns with KV cold misses — first token hits full attention compute. if KV is warm, subsequent tokens are much faster.
[03:12] Maya Chen: Diego, maybe show a quick diagram of cache warm vs cold?
[03:18] Diego Ramos: sure — (describes) warm path: cache hit -> KV lookup -> fast kernel path; cold path: run full attention, potential quantized kernel fallback if certain fused kernels not applicable; that adds 3-6x time depending on sequence length.
[03:34] Ethan Miles: we also saw higher tails when we enable quantization to int8 for cost savings — maybe the PQ or dequant path is slower sometimes?
[03:41] Diego Ramos: good point. quantization reduces memory but can change kernel selection. sometimes the runtime takes a fallback to a less-optimized kernel for certain seq lengths or layer boundary conditions — that creates jitter.
[03:54] Maya Chen: so for recommendations: pin model instances for steady-state, enable KV cache for chat-style workloads, and configure quantization profiles and check kernel compatibility for your sequence lengths.
[04:10] Laura Patel: about network hops — our egress to the model fleet is via a transit gateway with NAT — that could add 5-30ms but not 800ms. could routing cause the big spikes?
[04:22] Diego Ramos: large spikes more likely from compute or cold spikes, but combined with a long GC or node-level scheduling it can amplify. also if a request gets routed to a different availability zone and the client waits, that extra hop can push p99 higher.
[04:38] Priya Singh: what about batching? we use dynamic batching at the inference gateway with a max wait of 40ms — could that cause tail effects?
[04:47] Diego Ramos: dynamic batching reduces cost but introduces jitter. if your request arrival pattern has bursts, the batching window can sometimes hold requests slightly longer; also continuous batching in the runtime tries to aggregate but respects latency SLOs. If you need tighter p95/p99, decrease max batch wait or move to instance-level pinned batching.
[05:04] Ethan Miles: we're worried about cost though — smaller batch windows = more compute cost.
[05:11] Maya Chen: that's the classic tradeoff: latency vs cost. Redwood Optimize can simulate cost/latency tradeoffs given your trace to recommend batch windows and quantization. we can run that for you.
[05:24] Laura Patel: can you run a runbook on best configs? like what to change first to see impact on p99?
[05:30] Diego Ramos: yes — quick runbook I'd propose: 1) enable KV cache and warm it with representative traces; 2) pin a small pool of instances to remove cold scheduling; 3) run a quantization compatibility test with your seq-length distribution; 4) lower batch max-wait for critical endpoints; 5) capture perf traces and histogram of kernels used.
[05:50] Priya Singh: when you say warm cache, how long does warming take and how persistent is it across restarts?
[05:58] Diego Ramos: depends on workload size; small chat contexts can warm in minutes with synthetic replay. cache persists in-memory per model process - if you scale down to zero it will be cold. dedicated pools avoid that.
[06:12] Ethan Miles: about streaming vs non-streaming: our clients time out if first token >300ms — any tips?
[06:19] Diego Ramos: for strict first-token SLOs: 1) prefer pinned instances and warm KV; 2) use non-quantized fast kernel for first-token path or a hybrid flow where first token uses fp16 path then switch; 3) reduce batching wait for that endpoint; 4) consider pre-fetching or predictively warming common prefixes.
[06:40] Laura Patel: is that hybrid path something Redwood supports?
[06:44] Maya Chen: yes, we can do per-route runtime profiles; some customers keep a small fp16 pool for latency-sensitive first-token and route lower-priority requests to quantized pools.
[06:54] Ethan Miles: network-wise, what's the worst we should expect for VPC->hosted cross-region?
[06:59] Diego Ramos: cross-region adds 50-150ms typically; inside-region VPC with transit gw is usually 10-40ms. big p99s >500ms are usually compute/scheduling.
[07:11] Priya Singh: ok, let's walk through an example. we had a 13B model, seq length 512, batch size variable. p50 110ms, p95 300ms, p99 950ms. what might happen at layer/kernel level?
[07:26] Diego Ramos: layer-level: when sequence long and KV cold, you compute full attention for all layers, which triggers larger matmuls and maybe different kernel tiling that aren't as optimized. plus memory allocation jitter. if quantized, some layers may use slower dequant/quant routines. combined you get nonlinear increases in time.
[07:47] Maya Chen: Diego, do you have suggestions for kernel-level tuning?
[07:50] Diego Ramos: yes — ensure kernels are pinned to CUDA versions that match our build; for certain seq-lengths some cuBLAS/hip kernels are faster. we can recommend a kernel-selection profile. also pre-allocate KV buffers and reuse them to avoid alloc pauses.
[08:06] Laura Patel: our ops team saw some GC spikes in the Java orchestrator — could that line up?
[08:11] Priya Singh: yeah we saw node memory reclaim events occasionally.
[08:14] Diego Ramos: that would absolutely appear as latency spikes. JVM GC or kube kubelet eviction can block threads leading to long tails. we recommend isolating inference processes from control-plane and ensuring memory overcommit is low.
[08:28] Ethan Miles: would on-prem help reduce p99?
[08:32] Maya Chen: on-prem reduces network variability but you still have the same runtime concerns. it helps if your network is deterministic and you control scaling. Redwood Private offers a private control plane plus recommended configs.
[08:44] Laura Patel: let's talk about measurement — what metrics should we capture to pinpoint p99 source?
[08:50] Diego Ramos: capture per-request timeline: enqueue time, batch start, kernel selection, KV hit/miss flag, model compute time, serialization, network RTT, and container scheduling events. histograms for kernel durations and percentiles.
[09:05] Maya Chen: also collect phase markers: first-token latency, subsequent-token average, and per-layer times if possible.
[09:12] Ethan Miles: we can add markers in our SDK, we have distributed tracing.
[09:16] Diego Ramos: perfect; instrument traces with those markers and share. we'll correlate with our runtime logs to find exact kernel fallbacks.
[09:26] Laura Patel: any quick wins we can try today?
[09:29] Maya Chen: yes — 1) pin a tiny warm pool for your most latency-sensitive route; 2) enable runtime KV cache and run a warm-up trace; 3) run the quantization compatibility test on a staging trace; 4) lower batching window for that route.
[09:43] Ethan Miles: about warm-up — do you have tooling to replay traces?
[09:46] Diego Ramos: yes we can replay traces into the dedicated pool to warm the KV caches and replicate your arrival pattern. we'll need the traces and a short window for run.
[09:56] Priya Singh: how intrusive is kernel probe? you mentioned kernel-selection profiling.
[10:00] Diego Ramos: it's non-invasive; we gather runtime counters and logs native to the runtime. no code change required, just a debug toggle.
[10:09] Laura Patel: we also saw tail when multi-tenant; could noisy neighbors cause these peaks?
[10:14] Diego Ramos: yes, if you share a GPU instance and the runtime schedules tasks from multiple models you can see interference. dedicated pools or stricter cgroup/cooldown settings help.
[10:26] Maya Chen: Tina (not on call) runs our Optimize engine to recommend batching and quant profiles — Diego can export a config for Ionix.
[10:34] Diego Ramos: i'll prepare a config template with batch windows, pin counts, and quant flags.
[10:39] Ethan Miles: we have a question on streaming: token-by-token vs chunked streaming — is chunked streaming better for first-token latency?
[10:47] Diego Ramos: chunked streaming where the runtime sends the first N tokens asap and then chunks reduces round-trips and can hide some jitter; it's a client-side tradeoff too.
[10:55] Priya Singh: any specifics on buffer sizes? we saw clients block when small chunks arrive.
[10:59] Diego Ramos: choose chunk sizes that align with your client render latency — 16-32 tokens is common, but test. smaller chunks mean more network overhead; larger chunks increase first-token delay if you wait for them.
[11:13] Maya Chen: ok let's tie back to the action items and next steps. Diego will run bench with KV on; Ethan will share traces and topology; Maya will send SOC2 and pricing.
[11:23] Laura Patel: yep that works. also can you include config snippets for the runtime and the gateway?
[11:28] Diego Ramos: yes sample config and command lines will be in the spreadsheet.
[11:33] Ethan Miles: about quantization — any accuracy drop we should expect with int8 for our 13B model?
[11:39] Diego Ramos: depends on model type; many instruction-tuned models degrade slightly but often within acceptable tolerance. we recommend running a quality eval with your prompts. Redwood Optimize will run both perf and eval to recommend a profile.
[11:53] Priya Singh: timeline for the pilot?
[11:55] Maya Chen: Diego can run bench by 3/31; if traces arrive by 3/28 we can do a pilot the week of 3/29.
[12:04] Laura Patel: good. one more question: are there known issues with KV cache persistence across redeploys?
[12:10] Diego Ramos: by default cache is in-process. if you redeploy you'll lose it unless using dedicated pool or shared external cache feature (we have an optional persistent cache in Private customers).
[12:22] Ethan Miles: can you share perf logs that show kernel fallback examples?
[12:26] Diego Ramos: yes, we'll include examples in the spreadsheet.
[12:30] Maya Chen: cool. any other blockers?
[12:32] Laura Patel: none from me. we'll gather traces.
[12:35] Priya Singh: ok thanks.
[12:37] Maya Chen: great, we'll recap in an email with artifacts. thanks, everyone.
